items.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

items.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
items.summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

items.title: Training Agents to Fail Predictably: Fine-Tuning for Forecastable Tail Risk
items.summary: Before deployment, an AI system might be evaluated on thousands or even millions of inputs, but after deployment it may encounter billions, so its worst failures may not appear during evaluation. Jones et al. (2025) proposed forecasting how risky the riskiest deployment inputs will be by scoring how close the system comes to failure on each evaluation input and extrapolating from the highest scores. We show that the error of this forecast splits into a noise term, whose distribution is the same for every model up to scale, and terms that depend on the shape of the tail of the model's risk scores. These model-dependent terms can make the forecast under-predict badly, both in theory, whenever the evaluation set lacks a rare kind of input that deployment contains, and in practice: on real user prompts marked as toxic, the forecast under-predicted the probability that a response begins with an offensive word for all eleven language models we tested. Because the shape of this tail is a property of the model, we propose fine-tuning the model itself to make the forecast accurate, using the forecast error as the training loss. In a model organism of jailbreaking and in an RL gridworld with rare traps, our method reduced the held-out squared forecast error by factors of 14 to 60, lowered worst-case risk about as much as direct risk minimization (or more), and preserved the model's primary behavior. For settings in which the model should change as little as possible, we show that training with an alternative safety constraint and an added loss term improved the forecast with far smaller changes to the model. Our method also improved the forecast in RL from sampled returns, in language models of up to 8B parameters, and (with minimal-change training) on the toxic user prompts.

items.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
items.summary: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

items.title: Superplatforms are Strategically Compelled to Counteract AI Agents
items.summary: Over the past decades, superplatforms, digital companies that integrate a vast range of third-party services and applications into a single, unified ecosystem, have built their fortunes on monopolizing user attention through targeted advertising and algorithmic content curation. Yet the emergence of AI agents driven by large language models (LLMs) threatens to upend this business model. Agents can not only free user attention with autonomy across diverse platforms and therefore bypass the user-attention-based monetization, but might also become the new entrance for digital traffic. Hence, we argue that superplatforms have to attack AI agents to defend their centralized control of digital traffic entrance. Specifically, we analyze the fundamental conflict between user-attention-based monetization and agent-driven autonomy through the lens of our gatekeeping theory. We show how AI agents can disintermediate superplatforms and potentially become the next dominant gatekeepers, thereby forming the urgent necessity for superplatforms to proactively constrain and attack AI agents. Moreover, we go through the potential technologies for superplatform-initiated attacks, covering a brand-new, unexplored technical area with unique challenges. We have to emphasize that, despite our position, this paper does not advocate for adversarial attacks by superplatforms on AI agents, but rather offers an envisioned trend to highlight the emerging tensions between superplatforms and AI agents. Our aim is to raise awareness and encourage critical discussion for collaborative solutions, prioritizing user interests and perserving the openness of digital ecosystems in the age of AI agents.

items.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
items.summary: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds together, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Reconstructed from real materials with 13 domain experts, its 11 projects span settings such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting. They comprise 150 subtasks, with 2-15 subsequent releases of new materials and client feedback per project. Later subtasks build on the agent's own earlier deliverables, so unresolved errors can carry into downstream work. Expert rubrics assess each subtask submission and the final delivery package. Across seven model-harness systems, the best scores 65.0/100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery; delivery also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

items.title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
items.summary: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

items.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
items.summary: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.

items.title: Bench-MFG: A Benchmark Suite for Learning in Stationary Mean Field Games
items.summary: The rise of Mean Field Games (MFGs) has fostered a growing family of algorithms designed to solve large-scale multi-agent systems. However, the field currently lacks a standardized evaluation protocol, forcing researchers to rely on bespoke, isolated, and often simplistic environments. This fragmentation makes it difficult to assess the robustness, generalization, and failure modes of emerging methods. To address this gap, we propose a comprehensive benchmark suite for MFGs, focusing on the discrete-time, discrete-space, stationary setting. We introduce a taxonomy of problem classes, ranging from no-interaction and monotone games to potential and dynamics-coupled games, and provide prototypical environments for each. Furthermore, we present MF-Garnets, a method for generating random MFG instances to facilitate rigorous statistical testing. We benchmark a variety of learning algorithms across these environments, including a novel population-based approach (MF-PSO). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark for MFGs.

items.title: Integrated hybrid edge-cloud architecture for multi-robot and human-robot collaboration using ROS 2-MQTT-FIWARE in Mediterranean Greenhouses
items.summary: The imperative to develop more sustainable agriculture demands a transition from isolated automation toward the deployment of multi-robot systems (MRS) in agrifood environments. However, Mediterranean greenhouse settings-characterized by narrow corridors, dense biomass, and structural metallic interference-pose significant challenges for robust and scalable communication between agents. Traditional robotic frameworks, such as ROS 2, frequently encounter node discovery issues and latency spikes due to dynamic obstacles, dense foliage, and other characteristic greenhouse elements, creating a critical bottleneck for real-time coordination. This paper proposes an innovative cloud-based hybrid architecture that establishes a two-way communication bridge between ROS 2, acting as an edge computing platform, and iVeg as a Decision Support System (DSS), using MQTT and the European FIWARE platform. The proposed framework enables seamless interoperability between fleets of multiple robots in environments with communication constraints, facilitating the synchronised exchange of high-level telemetry, point cloud data and farmer identification for collaboration, amongst other critical data. The architecture was validated in a high-fidelity simulation environment and subsequently tested in a real-world greenhouse scenario, demonstrating its ability to maintain persistent connectivity and data integrity under adverse network conditions. The results indicate that the integration of MQTT effectively eliminates information silos, providing a scalable and decentralised solution for managing complex robotic missions, which are executed locally via Edge Computing. This work sets a new methodological precedent for the concept of Greenhouse Models as a Service (GMaaS), bridging the gap between low-level robotic control and high-level, cloud-based IoT decision-making.

items.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

input.content: Nhóm 3 người đi ăn hết 500, cafe hết 200, nhậu hết 300.
Trung đã trả 300, Đức trả 700 phần còn lại. Tính xem giờ ai gửi ai bao nhiêu tiền?

result.actual_text:
Để tính xem ai gửi ai bao nhiêu tiền, trước tiên ta cần xác định tổng chi phí và số tiền mà mỗi người đã trả.

1. **Tổng chi phí**:
   - Ăn: 500
   - Cafe: 200
   - Nhậu: 300
   - **Tổng cộng**: 500 + 200 + 300 = 1000

2. **Số tiền đã trả**:
   - Trung: 300
   - Đức: 700
   - **Tổng số tiền đã trả**: 300 + 700 = 1000 (đúng với tổng chi phí)

3. **Phân chia chi phí**:
   - Mỗi người sẽ phải trả: 1000 / 3 = 333.33 (khoảng 333.33 cho mỗi người)

4. **Tính số tiền cần gửi**:
   - Trung đã trả 300, nên Trung cần trả thêm: 333.33 - 300 = 33.33
   - Đức đã trả 700, nên Đức đã trả thừa: 700 - 333.33 = 366.67

**Kết luận**:
- Trung cần gửi cho Đức: 33.33
- Đức sẽ nhận từ Trung: 33.33

Vậy Trung sẽ gửi cho Đức 33.33.
